abstract.title: Abstract
abstract.p: The discovery of the glymphatic system and meningeal lymphatic vessels revolutionized the understanding of brain waste clearance. These findings challenged the long-held notion of CNS immune privilege and provided insights into how the brain maintains homeostasis despite lacking conventional lymphatic drainage. However, the impact of pathological conditions, particularly CNS cancers, on the glymphatic system and vice versa remains underexplored.

Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common and aggressive primary adult CNS cancer. Its presence results in glymphatic dysfunction with significant clinical implications. Recent studies suggest that the glymphatic system interacts with GBM to influence immunity, drug delivery, fluid regulation and tumour progression, stressing its significant role in GBM biology and potentially treatment response.

This review highlights the evidence for glymphatic dysfunction in GBM and its consequences. Furthermore, we discuss the potential to harness the power of the glymphatic system to improve patient outcomes in this terrible disease.

sec.p: Keywords: glymphatic system, glioma, glioblastoma, meningeal lymphatic system, immunology

abstract.p: The glymphatic system clears waste and regulates fluid and immune dynamics in the brain, but its function is disrupted in glioblastoma. Soumbasis et al. examine the effects of this dysfunction on tumour progression, immune responses, and the effectiveness of therapeutic interventions.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Glioblastoma (GBM) is the most common and unfortunately, most aggressive primary brain tumour in adults, with a median survival of only 14.6 months despite surgery and chemoradiation.1 Disease progression, treatment effects and cerebral oedema significantly impair quality of life and survival in GBM.2-4 However, mechanistic connections between the tumour microenvironment and patient outcomes are still poorly understood.

While the GBM microenvironment has been extensively profiled, the glymphatic system remains underexplored. Unlike peripheral tissues that rely on lymphatic vasculature for macroscopic waste clearance,5 fluid regulation6 and immunomodulation,6 the brain relies on the glymphatic system for these functions. As such, glymphatic pathways consisting of perivascular networks are essential for maintaining homeostasis and can influence drug delivery and immunity in the brain. GBM compromises the glymphatic system, causing dysfunction that has the potential to adversely affect patients.

Reduced fluid turnover resulting from glymphatic dysfunction in GBM may influence disease progression. GBM is associated with cerebral oedema and elevated intracranial pressures that lead to decreased CSF production. Combined with glymphatic dysfunction and impaired fluid outflow, the rate of cerebral fluid turnover is lowered. These fluid dynamics facilitate the build-up of toxic proteins and cytokines, creating an immune-dysregulated microenvironment with the potential to hasten GBM progression.

In this review article, we explore the clinically relevant anatomy of the glymphatic system, how glymphatic function is measured, the function of the glymphatic system in GBM preclinical models and patients and the downstream consequences of altered immunity, drug delivery, fluid regulation and tumour growth. This review aims to summarize the rapidly growing literature investigating the connection between GBM and the glymphatic system, emphasizing the importance of understanding this system to develop better treatments for this terrible disease.

sec.title: Anatomy of the glymphatic system
sec.p: The glymphatic system is a macroscopic waste clearance pathway that removes soluble proteins, metabolites and facilitates immune cell trafficking in the CNS.5,7 The anatomy of the glymphatic system uniquely positions it to carry out these functions (Fig. 1).

sec.p: In most vascularized tissues, the lymphatic vessels parallel the blood vasculature, participating in the filtering of proteins and solutes. However, the brain lacks the traditional lymphatic vessels found in peripheral tissues, posing a challenge for the rapid clearance of interstitial fluid (ISF) and solutes despite the high metabolic activity of the CNS.8 CSF is a distinct component of the CNS that helps fulfil the role of solute clearance. CSF is produced in the choroid plexus and flows through cerebral ventricles and the subarachnoid space, where it interfaces with the brain parenchyma and glymphatic system. CSF egress then occurs through arachnoid villi found along the venous sinuses, where it is partially reabsorbed into the bloodstream.9 Waste clearance of the brain parenchyma is postulated to occur via convective bulk flow of ISF diffusely throughout the brain tissue, with subsequent drainage into the CSF.

At a microscopic level, the glymphatic system is composed of perivascular spaces, also known as Virchow-Robin spaces (Fig. 2). All vasculature within the brain parenchyma, including arterioles, capillaries and venules, are surrounded by astrocytic end feet, which create the outer wall of the perivascular space.7 The perivascular space is also bounded by perivascular stromal cells, including fibroblasts, pericytes, vascular smooth muscle cells, and immune cells such as macrophages, in between the endothelial membrane and astrocytic end feet.10-13 Supplied by the internal carotid and vertebral arteries, as the cerebral circulation becomes penetrating arterioles, which dive through the brain parenchyma, the perivascular space becomes continuous with the basal lamina. Therefore, at the capillary level, the perivascular space consists solely of basal lamina and perivascular stromal cells.7,10,11 In the perivascular spaces next to arteries and veins, where space is more abundant, CSF enters and fills those spaces via a porous basal lamina, which offers minimal resistance to CSF influx due to its loose fibrous matrix.7

It is located between the vascular endothelium and the astrocytic end-feet expressing AQP4 channels, which form the outer boundary of the space. CSF enters periarterial spaces through arterial pulsatility, respiration and pressure gradients, facilitating solute exchange before being cleared via perivenous and perineural efflux pathways into the meningeal lymphatics and deep cervical lymph nodes. sec.p: CSF and ISF continuously exchange within the brain’s perivascular spaces.5 CSF from the subarachnoid space is propelled into the periarterial spaces by arterial pulsatility, respiration and CSF pressure gradients, creating a convective influx. From this periarterial space, CSF is transported into the brain parenchyma through aquaporin-4 (AQP4) water channels expressed in astrocytic end feet lining the brain vasculature and perivascular space. Here, solutes and metabolites are exchanged between ISF and CSF. CSF influx concurrently drives ISF movement towards the perivenous spaces surrounding the large draining cerebral veins.5 Finally, the ISF collects in the perivenous space before being shuttled out of the brain toward the cervical lymphatic system through mechanisms that remain unclear.14-16 Overall, this macroscopic waste clearance system, characterized by convective fluid fluxes across glial AQP4 channels, has been coined the ‘glymphatic system’.

It is important to note that convective fluid fluxes are not the only brain solute and waste clearance mechanisms at play. Tracers were shown to clear out of murine brains along the tunica media of arteries and capillary basement membranes instead of the veins,17,18 supporting the intramural periarterial drainage (IPAD) hypothesis.17 The distribution of amyloid-β deposition in the brains of cerebral amyloid angiopathy and Alzheimer’s disease patients supports the drainage patterns predicted by IPAD.19 To demonstrate that arterial pulsations were not critical to IPAD fluid dynamics, a key process propelling glymphatic perivenous efflux, mathematical modelling, followed by pulse modulator use in mice, demonstrated that IPAD occurred independently of changes in pulsations.20 Furthermore, solutes were shown to exit within the walls of arteries retrograde to the direction of blood flow.17 Thus, brain solute and waste clearance via IPAD mechanisms are distinct from the convective fluid forces associated with the glymphatic system. Another waste clearance mechanism involves diffusive fluid forces travelling along concentration gradients, aided by oscillatory mixing, driven by cardiac pulsatility and arterial smooth muscle contractions.21,22 The combined effect of diffusion and mixing is known as ‘dispersion’ and has been demonstrated computationally.23 Investigators must work towards defining the relative contributions of glymphatic, IPAD and mixing mechanisms, as their precise roles in maintaining CNS homeostasis and their pathological relevance remain unclear. While our review focuses on glymphatic mechanisms, we direct you to several excellent reviews critically appraising the evidence supporting these models of brain solute and waste clearance, with some proposing hybrid frameworks incorporating aspects from each model.21,24-26

How CSF drains into cervical lymph nodes is also an active area of study. A lymphatic vessel network near blood vessels and cranial nerves within the dura mater of mice has been described.27 These ‘meningeal lymphatic vessels’ absorb CSF from nearby subarachnoid spaces and brain ISF via the glymphatic system and transport this fluid to deep cervical lymph nodes (dcLNs) through skull base foramina. Supporting this, CSF drainage into meningeal lymphatic vessels was shown to occur primarily into dural sinuses and along cranial nerves.8 Perineural efflux pathways were observed mainly along the trigeminal, glossopharyngeal, vagal and spinal accessory nerves.28 While the exact anatomic connection between cranial nerves and meningeal lymphatic vessels is still unknown, continuity of the cranial nerve epineurium with dura mater29 suggests that meningeal lymphatic vessels serve as extensions of the peripheral lymphatic system, bridging macromolecule transport from the brain to extracranial lymphatics.30 Overall, the glymphatic system is composed of distinct anatomical components that connect the fluid compartment bathing the brain parenchyma with the peripheral lymphatic system.

sec.title: Functioning of the glymphatic system under homeostatic conditions
sec.p: The glymphatic system plays a crucial role in maintaining brain health and function. There have been many excellent reviews on the homeostatic functions of the glymphatic system, and thus we will keep our discussion brief.7,30,31 One of the major roles of the glymphatic system is to clear metabolic brain waste products at night.32 The glymphatic system exports potassium, lactate and proteins such as amyloid-β and tau.33,34 Ultimately, fluid carrying these molecules and wastes is directed towards the venous system. Concurrently, the glymphatic system delivers nutrients such as glucose35 and fat36 via the exchange of CSF and ISF. Balancing waste clearance with solute and nutrient delivery helps maintain osmotic pressure in the CNS.7

Alongside the distribution of molecules and macromolecules to and from the CNS, the glymphatic system regulates the amount of cerebral fluid within the rigid confines of the skull. Several proteins, including AQP4,37 α1-syntrophin,38 dystrophin,39 laminin,40 glucose transporter proteins41 and connexin-3042,43 in astrocytic end feet are polarized. Loss of this polarization is associated with impaired fluid homeostasis and neurologic disorders.39,44-46 However, many studies have shown AQP4 channels play the largest role in cerebral water homeostasis by transporting water at speeds up to 3 × 109 molecules per second.47-49 The effects of eliminating AQP4 in model organisms result in prolonged ISF clearance,50 water retention and increased intracranial pressures.51 Thus, AQP4-mediated water transport is vital to CNS fluid regulation and glymphatic system function.

Glymphatic system function may affect neuronal activity. During non-REM sleep52 and anaesthesia,53 glymphatic flow increases, upregulating CSF volumes in the brain. This CSF volume expansion could enhance the distribution of signalling molecules across greater distances. Since classical neuromodulators such as acetylcholine, noradrenaline and serotonin are produced by cells close to the ventricular ependyma or pial lining of the brain surface, which are CSF reservoirs,53 the glymphatic system is an obvious anatomical conduit potentially subserving signalling functions. For instance, the hypothalamus, located by the third ventricle, secretes neuropeptide Y, pro-opiomelanocortin, arginine vasopressin, vasoactive intestinal peptide and oxytocin, all of which can be found in the CSF.54-57 CSF-mediated signals could not only be distributed throughout the brain via the glymphatic system but also into the gut–brain axis.31

Lastly, the glymphatic system also serves an important role in CNS immunity. The meningeal lymphatic vessels connect the glymphatic system to the deep cervical lymph nodes,58 acting as immune surveillance gateways for T cells and myeloid cells.59 This link to the perivascular space is a route for immune cell trafficking.59 Altered glymphatic function under pathological conditions could potentially exacerbate inflammatory responses, promote the accumulation of metabolic and immune byproducts that are implicated in neurodegeneration and contribute to immune dysregulation. For further details, we refer you to the excellent reviews by Hablitz and Nederguard,31 Nycz and Mandera,60 and Louveau et al.61 on immune homeostasis in the glymphatic system.
In sum, the glymphatic system plays major homeostatic roles in waste clearance, nutrient delivery, fluid regulation, immunity and potentially neurotransmitter signalling.

sec.title: Imaging of the glymphatic system
sec.p: Imaging is a key technique for studying the glymphatic system (Table 1). The glymphatic system was first visualized in vivo by Iliff et al.62 using a combination of two-photon microscopy and fluorescent tracers in mice. Tracers were injected into the CSF of the cisterna magna and tracked as they entered the brain parenchyma, demonstrating that CSF distribution into the brain is not random, but rapidly directed by astrocytic end feet along perivascular spaces next to cortical pial arteries and penetrating arterioles. MRI with or without contrast agents or tracers can also be used to non-invasively visualize the glymphatic system.62,63 Tracer-based or contrast-enhanced MRI (CE-MRI) can map fluid flow and drainage pathways by tracking dye movement through sequential scans.63 One of the most common contrast-based measures, delayed tissue enhancement (DTE), quantifies the uptake of gadolinium-based contrast agent in brain parenchyma following intravenous administration. As gadolinium does not cross the blood–brain barrier (BBB), uptake in brain tissue is due to glymphatic exchange between CSF and ISF, providing a measure of glymphatic function.64 This DTE is first visible approximately 30 min after injection, peaking at 90 min.64 Beyond DTE, MRI-derived bulk flow velocities65 and diffusion tensor imaging along the perivascular space (DTI-ALPS)66 provide surrogate measures of glymphatic function. DTI-ALPS yields an index correlating with glymphatic clearance by exploiting the fact that white matter fibres contributing to anisotropic diffusion run perpendicular to the perivascular space along periventricular medullary veins. However, due to the millimetre-level resolution of diffusion imaging, DTI-ALPS cannot distinguish whether fluid movement is inside or outside the perivascular space or differentiate periarterial from perivenous flow. Consequently, DTI-ALPS reflects macroscopic, directionally preferential diffusion, rather than active glymphatic flow.67 Additionally, because DTI-ALPS typically uses a single-shell acquisition with a high b-value (approximately 1000 s/mm2), it emphasizes restricted diffusion, potentially underrepresenting the dynamics of free water, such as ISF and CSF. This limitation may obscure slower or bulk fluid movement, and the lack of multi-shell data prevents separation of distinct diffusion components.67 Although DTI-ALPS is a limited and indirect measure of glymphatic function, it correlates with function and is easy to calculate.67 Encouragingly, there is a strong concordance between DTI-ALPS and intrathecal CE-MRI.66 DTI-ALPS has been used to quantify glymphatic function in patients with many conditions, including Alzheimer’s disease, type 2 diabetes mellitus, ischaemic stroke, Parkinson’s disease and cancer-related pain syndromes,63,68,69 but imaging studies of the glymphatic system in neuro-oncology remain comparatively sparse.70

sec.p: A more recent advancement in studying the glymphatic system involves the use of light-sheet fluorescence microscopy (LSFM) of optically cleared brains.71 LSFM is an advanced imaging technique that uses a thin sheet of light to illuminate one plane within a sample while capturing the fluorescence emitted. Sheets of light can be scanned widely and rapidly, generating high-resolution, 3D images. Thus, LSFM excels in imaging large volumes at high speed and is particularly valuable for identifying regional differences in glymphatic activity.71

Other imaging techniques used to study glymphatic function include PET, single-photon emission computed tomography (SPECT), autoradiography and transcranial Doppler ultrasound,72 although these are less commonly used. The pros and cons of the various glymphatic imaging techniques are shown in Table 1. Together, these imaging techniques have confirmed the anatomical pathways for fluid flow through the glymphatic system and brain parenchyma.62,63,73

sec.title: Evidence for glymphatic dysfunction in glioblastoma
sec.p: Imaging studies of the glymphatic system in GBM have demonstrated impairment at the CSF, ISF and outflow levels. These altered fluid dynamics may be causes and consequences of cerebral oedema and raised intracranial pressures, secondary to GBM-associated inflammation, angiogenesis and growth.74,75 Although raised intracranial pressure is well-documented in tumour-bearing animal models, the pathophysiologic link to disruption of glymphatic clearance pathways is in the process of being established.

A substantial portion of the work investigating glymphatic dysfunction in GBM has been performed in animal models. Contrast-enhanced MRI with intra-cisterna magna gadolinium infusion and advanced kinetic modelling reveals significantly reduced CSF influx, impaired CSF/ISF clearance and increased gadolinium retention in GBM-bearing rats compared to controls, indicating glymphatic system dysfunction.74 Compromised gadolinium efflux along the optic nerves also suggests disrupted glymphatic system outflow.74 A more granular investigation of ISF flow was undertaken using a gadolinium-based contrast agent, gadobenate dimeglumine.76 The direction of ISF flow was found to be heterogeneous within and around tumours,76 challenging previous assumptions of outward fluid flow due to the higher ISF pressures measured within tumours versus surrounding tissues.77 Fluid flow direction was independent of tumour size,76 suggesting that glymphatic system impairment may arise from tumour-intrinsic factors beyond mere physical invasion or compression of perivascular spaces. Additionally, in rats bearing thalamic GBMs, altered drainage routes in the nearby caudate indicated ISF changes extend beyond the tumour site and may have wide-ranging effects.78 The dynamics of ISF flow have been linked to tumour invasion79 and shaping of the cancer microenvironment,80 highlighting the need to account for the complexity of fluid flow at the CSF/ISF and outflow levels when investigating tumour invasion.

In a study examining glymphatic system outflow pathways, it was found that despite an extensive tumour-associated blood vessel network, CSF outflow still proceeds via meningeal lymphatic vessels and along exiting cranial nerves.81 MRI of CSF tracer P40D680 post-cisterna magna injection revealed dramatically diminished CSF drainage along cranial nerves and downstream lymph nodes in tumour-bearing animals compared to controls.81 Furthermore, tracer accumulation in the spine, accompanied by significant outflow from the sacral region, suggests compensatory mechanisms for impeded CSF outflow in the presence of GBM. Altogether, these findings suggest GBM blocks CSF outflow in the cranial cavity, which is partially compensated for by glymphatic outflow from the spinal compartment, implying that an ideal assay for measuring glymphatic function would include both the cranial and spinal compartments.

Imaging of the glymphatic system has also been tied to molecular changes in astrocytic end feet. In GBM-bearing rats, gadolinium-based contrast injected into the cisterna magna confirmed reduced CSF signal along the exiting cranial nerves.75 In a parallel group, Evans Blue injection into the cisterna magna with AQP4 co-staining showed diminished cranial nerve staining and a downregulation of AQP4 expression in astrocytic end feet within tumour regions compared to non-tumour regions.75 These findings link glymphatic dysfunction to reduced AQP4 expression.

In human GBM analysis, imaging studies also support the occurrence of glymphatic dysfunction.70,82 Real-time glymphatic drainage in human GBM was measured using peritumoural injections of the tracer, 99mTc-tilmanocept, followed by planar scintigraphy or SPECT, demonstrating impairment of tracer clearance.83 Retrospective analysis of 201 glioma patient MRIs with DTI-ALPS revealed lower DTI-ALPS values in GBM, a World Health Organization (WHO) grade 4 glioma, compared to lower WHO grade 2 and 3 gliomas, suggesting greater glymphatic impairment with increasing tumour grade and aggressiveness.68 Another study using DTI-ALPS to compare tumour-affected versus non-affected cerebral hemispheres in 24 patients, 10 of whom had GBMs, found DTI-ALPS was significantly decreased in the tumour-affected hemisphere, indicating spatial regulation of glymphatic system impairment.84 A prospective study measuring DTI-ALPS paired with analysis of AQP4 levels in brain tumours, including gliomas, revealed an inverse relationship between tumour size and predicted glymphatic system function, along with compensatory increases in AQP4 expression in tumour-adjacent brain regions.76

However, studies using DTI-ALPS in glioblastoma patients must be interpreted with caution. Structural distortion of brain tissue by glioblastoma due to mass effect, peritumoural oedema and direct infiltration, especially of white matter tracts, may distort diffusion metrics, compromising the robustness of DTI-ALPS indices.67 To mitigate these limitations, some studies attempt to use contralateral hemispheric comparisons or exclude abnormal tissues,84 but it is unclear whether contralateral hemispheres represent true normal controls and often abnormal tissues are regions of interest. Perhaps a more effective, broadly applicable strategy is to statistically adjust for fractional anisotropy and mean diffusivity.67 When this compensation is applied, reductions in DTI-ALPS indices persist, suggesting at least partial independence of DTI-ALPS measurements from deteriorations in white matter integrity.85 Uniform application of compensation strategies to DTI-ALPS measurements in glioblastoma patients, along with additional measures of glymphatic function, would enhance future studies.

Overall, imaging studies have documented glymphatic system dysfunction in human GBM, similar to that seen in other neurological diseases, including normal pressure hydrocephalus, idiopathic intracranial hypertension, stroke, subarachnoid haemorrhage, intracerebral haemorrhage and traumatic brain injury.70 However, the mechanisms underlying glymphatic dysfunction and its sequelae, especially in neuro-oncology, remain underexplored.

sec.title: The sequelae of glymphatic dysfunction in glioblastoma
sec.p: GBM-associated glymphatic dysfunction impairs immunosurveillance, exacerbates peritumoural oedema, disrupts drug delivery and potentially accelerates tumour invasion, all of which contribute to poor outcomes and diminish the quality of life of patients (Fig. 3).

sec.title: Glymphatic system dysfunction hinders immunosurveillance of glioblastoma
sec.p: The conventional paradigm of CNS immune privilege was based on a lack of lymphatic drainage from the CNS.86 However, discovery of the glymphatic system5 and meningeal lymphatic vessels27,59 sparked a surge of research into how antigenic material from the brain is transferred to peripheral lymphatic organs, where an immune reaction can be mounted.28

It is now widely acknowledged that under homeostatic conditions, immune cells actively patrol the meninges, providing CNS immune surveillance.28,30 Immune cells such as T cells, immature B cells and dendritic cells accumulate around dural sinuses where CSF is reabsorbed, then use meningeal lymphatic vessels for migration into the dcLNs, connecting the CNS and peripheral immune systems.28,30,87,88 However, the exact mechanisms governing when immune cells enter and exit brain parenchyma to perform immunosurveillance are still unclear,28 although due to anatomical links between the glymphatic system and meningeal lymphatic vessels, this process almost certainly involves perivascular pathways.

GBM immunosurveillance is impaired. During the early stages of GBM progression, neoplastic cells incite inflammatory responses characterized by local infiltration of innate immune cells such as macrophages and NK cells.89 These cells have antigen-presenting capabilities and may further activate cytotoxic T cell or humoral B cell responses aimed at restraining tumour growth.90 However, GBM quickly establishes a potently immunosuppressive microenvironment which evades immunosurveillance mechanisms,91-94 fostering immune tolerance and facilitating tumour progression.28 Aberrant expression of AQP4 in GBM contributes to the disruption of glymphatic transport and hinders the timely clearance of inflammatory factors produced by GBM and immune cells, contributing to immune dysregulation.95 Another study showed that after injecting the tracer 99mTc-tilmanocept into brain parenchyma adjacent to GBM, there was no signal detected in the dCLNs, despite the tracer’s high affinity for CD206,96,97 a receptor expressed by macrophages and dendritic cells. These findings suggest impaired trafficking of antigen-presenting cells in GBM. In sum, enhancing glymphatic outflow towards dCLNs may thus improve the clearance of metabolic wastes that promote tumour progression and potentiate immunosurveillance.83

Compromised glymphatic function also impairs meningeal lymphatic drainage, contributing to immunosuppression by limiting the transfer of tumour-specific antigens to dCLNs, leading to diminished activation of anti-tumoural T cells and weaker immunological responses.74,98 Ectopic expression of vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF)-C increased meningeal lymphatic drainage, enhancing CD8 T cell priming and migration of CD8 T cells into glioma, along with improving the efficacy of immune checkpoint blockade.98 In preclinical models, tumours overexpressing VEGF-C underwent meningeal lymphangiogenesis and became more sensitive to radiotherapy mediated by C-C motif chemokine ligand 21 (CCL21)-dependent dendritic cell trafficking and CD8 T cell activation.99 These results support VEGF-C as a candidate therapy for enhancing glymphatic and meningeal lymphatic function to improve anti-tumour innate and adaptive immunity. Ablation of dorsal meningeal lymphatics decreased the dissemination of antigenic murine GBM cells to the dCLNs, dendritic cell trafficking and the efficacy of anti-PD-1/CTLA-4 combination therapy.100 A phase II randomized controlled trial in recurrent GBM revealed that laser interstitial thermal therapy (LITT) synergizes with pembrolizumab, a PD-1 antagonist, significantly improving median survival101 in part by releasing large amounts of tumour antigen into the tumour microenvironment.102 Pairing dorsal meningeal lymphatic manipulation with LITT may prove synergistic and help overcome resistance to immune checkpoint therapies. Targeting AQP4 expression may also lead to anti-tumour immunomodulation, since AQP4 expression is significantly associated with the expression of multiple immune checkpoints, antigen presentation and immune cell effector genes.103 Combining inducible murine glioma models with commercially available genetic AQP4 knockouts104,105 could dissect the molecular mechanisms governing AQP4 expression and immunity. These results support an important link between glymphatic and meningeal lymphatic function and anti-GBM immunity, highlighting the potential to harness the glymphatic and meningeal lymphatic systems to bolster existing and experimental immunotherapies.

While augmenting glymphatic function and meningeal lymphatic drainage may lead to improved anti-tumour immunity, successful implementation of this strategy requires careful contextual application. Only ablating dorsal meningeal lymphatics inhibited tumour cell dissemination and dendritic cell trafficking in murine gliomas, not nasal or basal meningeal lymphatic manipulation,100 suggesting important regional differences in meningeal lymphatic roles. Enhancing nasal or basal meningeal lymphatics may be counterproductive to promoting tumour antigen-specific responses, since this diverts antigens away from dorsal meningeal lymphatics, a drainage pathway that mediates immune checkpoint therapy efficacy. Furthermore, expression of PD-L1 in lymph node-resident lymphatic endothelial cells restrains tumour-specific immunity by inducing apoptosis of tumour-specific CD8 central memory cells and immune tolerance in tumour-draining lymph nodes,106 suggesting a paradoxical pro-tumour consequence of enhancing glymphatic and meningeal lymphatic outflow. When considering treatments that alter this outflow, a delicate balance must be struck between increasing tumour antigen presentation and inhibiting anti-tumour immunity.

The glymphatic and meningeal lymphatic systems are actively involved in GBM immunosurveillance. While enhancing glymphatic and meningeal lymphatic outflow improves outcomes in murine glioma models, this has not been tested in patients, warranting urgent investigation.

sec.title: The influence of glymphatic dysfunction on drug delivery
sec.p: Systemically administered drugs face several obstacles to achieving therapeutic concentrations in the brain. For instance, the BBB represents a well-known obstacle to drug delivery, which has been covered in excellent reviews.107,108 Since drugs cannot diffuse freely from the circulation into brain parenchyma due to the BBB, drug delivery is restricted to cellular transport, preventing the vast majority of small-molecule drugs from reaching desired concentrations in the brain.109-111 The glymphatic system also influences drug delivery,112-117 adding another layer of complexity to achieving therapeutic CNS drug concentrations.

Glymphatic dysfunction in GBM is associated with high ISF pressures,51 which limits the transport of chemotherapies from the microvasculature into the brain tumour and drives these drugs into the surrounding parenchyma.118,119 The same outward convection current created by the differential pressures between the tumour and surrounding parenchyma facilitates drug removal, decreasing the tumour’s drug exposure time and subsequent efficacy.120

However, the convective circuit within the glymphatic system can also be harnessed as a drug delivery and distribution pathway. Studies investigating convection-enhanced delivery involving continuous infusion of therapeutic agents under positive pressure113,114 demonstrate that high ISF pressures can initially be overcome,121 but subsequent distribution still relies on arterial pulsations driving the agent through the perivascular spaces of the glymphatic system,112 underscoring the importance of the glymphatic system to drug delivery. The glymphatic system can also be manipulated with hyperosmotic therapy to increase the perivascular influx of therapeutics. Systemic administration of hypertonic saline increases plasma osmolality, lowers intracranial pressures and enhances the uptake of intracisternally-injected immunotherapies in mice.115 Similarly, systemic hypertonic saline significantly enhances the availability of intracisternally-administered radiotracer in rats, with a 3-fold increase in deep brain regions and a 5-fold increase in the cortex.115 Furthermore, tracer egress into the systemic circulation and elimination from the body slows.122 Thus, hypertonic saline may be a relatively easy method to enhance the glymphatic distribution of any drug delivered via CSF pathways and would be simple to administer alongside currently available chemotherapies for GBM. Another method known as ultrasound pulsation exploits the glymphatic system to improve drug delivery.116 By applying a single focused shockwave to the cranium, the blood–CSF barrier is opened, facilitating therapeutic delivery of previously CNS-impermeable drugs116 and enhancing drug-bearing CSF movement from periarterial to perivenous CSF spaces.117 In murine models of GBM, focused shockwave therapy achieved therapeutic concentrations of doxorubicin that suppressed tumour growth and prolonged survival.116 There are currently many trials investigating the ability of focused ultrasound to enhance drug delivery in GBM patients (NCT07179328, NCT07076472, NCT06496971, NCT04417088). Manipulating the brain-wide glymphatic system to enhance drug delivery is a promising avenue for combating the often inadequate distribution of anti-tumour drugs to patients.

sec.title: The glymphatic system and peritumoural oedema
sec.p: Aggressive brain tumours, such as GBM, induce peritumoural vasogenic oedema, which increases patient morbidity and mortality.123-125Disruption of the BBB leads to hydrostatic pressure differences between the vessel lumen and brain parenchyma. Subsequently, iso-osmotic fluid and serum proteins leak into the interstitial spaces of the brain,126 increasing intracranial pressures.81,123 Resultant neurologic deficits can dramatically threaten the outcome of GBM patients.

One study investigated the effect of AQP4 deletion on vasogenic oedema. Peritumoural vasogenic oedema, associated obstructive hydrocephalus, neurologic outcomes and the ability to clear oedema fluid were worse in AQP4-null mice, suggesting that oedema fluid is in part cleared by an AQP4-dependent mechanism.123,127

Conversely, studies comparing neoplastic to non-neoplastic human brain showed that AQP4 upregulation was observed in oedematous brain tumours and surrounding tissues and was correlated with increased BBB permeability.128 However, it is unclear whether AQP4 upregulation is a cause or consequence of impaired fluid clearance in conditions of cerebral oedema, potentially explaining the difference observed between murine and human studies. Human glioma patients with larger peritumoural oedema volumes have greater glymphatic system impairment as determined by DTI.68 A later volumetric MRI study confirmed the positive correlation between AQP4 expression and peritumoural oedema volume, as well as revealed larger CSF volumes82 in patients with brain tumours such as GBM. Overall, GBM and brain tumours are associated with peritumoural oedema and glymphatic system dysfunction, but whether AQP4 modulation in humans can improve fluid regulation to mitigate cerebral oedema warrants further research. One of the most common medications administered to reduce peritumoural oedema is the steroid, dexamethasone.129 Dexamethasone has been shown to modulate AQP4 expression in models of intracerebral haemorrhage,130 but this link in GBM has not been directly established and could help uncover the glymphatic mechanisms underlying peritumoural oedema in GBM patients.

sec.title: Glymphatic system involvement in GBM invasion, metastasis and treatment resistance
sec.p: The dynamics of fluid flow have been shown in non-CNS cancers to influence tumour invasion, proliferation and differentiation.79,131,132 For example, ISF flow increases the percentage of cells that become migratory, enhances migrational speed and introduces directional bias.79,131 On top of encouraging cancer cells to migrate in a certain direction, tumour cells can also express receptors that augment this migration. Breast carcinoma cell lines demonstrate a CCR7-dependent chemotaxis in the same direction as fluid flow.79 Fluid flow is postulated to drive a subpopulation of tumour cells, perhaps those with receptor-dependent chemotaxis, towards draining lymphatic vessels, which are a major route of metastasis.131 These fluid flow dynamics are reflected in CNS cancers.

CNS tumours exhibit elevated ISF pressures relative to normal tissue.133-135 Irregular cell growth, congestion and leaky blood vessels from tumour-associated angiogenesis drive this increased pressure and promote glymphatic fluid movement from the tumour into the surrounding interstitial space.72 This fluid movement, particularly at the tumour edges, has been associated with the formation of paracellular gradients driving tumour cell invasion.136,137 Paracellular gradients are established as ISF carries cell-secreted proteins, such as CXCL12, downstream of murine GBMs where they bind to the extracellular matrix. GBM cells expressing CXCR4 then participate in directional metastasis.138,139 Thus, by promoting migration, the convective flux within the glymphatic system may also contribute to invasion. To test whether modulating glymphatic flux mitigates these gradients and suppresses tumour progression, TGN-073, an AQP4 facilitator that promotes ISF circulation,140 is readily available and has been administered in rodent models of Alzheimer’s disease intraperitoneally with resultant enhanced glymphatic function.141

Subsequent glymphatic fluid drainage into the meningeal lymphatic vessels and deep cervical lymph nodes (dCLNs) could provide a route for CNS tumour metastasis. In mice, therapeutic disruption of dorsal meningeal lymphatic vessels (MLVs) impaired dissemination of GBM cells to dCLNs.100 A case study of a recurrent GBM patient with cervical lymphadenopathy revealed metastatic GBM cells within the lymph nodes,142 proving this route can be traversed by GBM in humans. Interestingly, extracranial metastasis of GBM occurs in less than 2% of cases,143 suggesting that factors beyond accessing the MLVs and dCLNs via the glymphatic system are at play in establishing new tumour foci.

Certain characteristics of the glymphatic system may promote GBM, once established. CSF within the glymphatic system can serve as reservoirs for pro-tumorigenic proteins secreted by GBM.121 The observation that patients with GBMs in proximity to the lateral ventricles have worse survival compared to those that are distant supports this notion.144 Vitronectin and matrix metalloproteinases, known to promote glioma cell migration, are found in the CSF of GBM patients.145,146 SERPINA3, a gene encoding α1-antichymotrypsin, is elevated in the CSF of GBM patients and associated with the promotion of cancer stem cells and tumour aggressiveness.147 Nuclear protein 1 (NUPR1) was identified as a mediator of chemoradiation and reduced survival in the CSF of GBM patients. CSF may also be a major mediator of intercellular communication in GBM patients. MicroRNA (miRNA)-containing extracellular vesicles are most abundant in CSF and not plasma.148 Since GBM cells are bathed in CSF and CSF and ISF are exchanged in the glymphatic system, there is a close interaction between GBM and the glymphatic system that may influence tumour progression and treatment response. In recognition of this, there are extensive ongoing efforts to diagnose and profile GBM via liquid biopsies of CSF.149 Understanding the interplay between GBM, CSF and the glymphatic system is crucial to developing reliable biomarkers and effective treatments for this disease.

sec.title: Conclusion
sec.p: The abysmal prognosis of glioblastoma despite multimodality treatments underscores the importance of better understanding its pathophysiology. Uncovering the role of the glymphatic system in GBM has important implications for immunity, treatment efficacy, peritumoural oedema and invasion, given its major homeostatic roles. Impaired CSF-ISF exchange within the glymphatic system instigates a cascade of events that can contribute to the malignancy of GBM, but the glymphatic system can also be harnessed to improve outcomes. Future efforts focusing on rejuvenating compromised glymphatic function hold great promise for opening new avenues to combat GBM. Ultimately, improved understanding of GBM-glymphatic biology could enhance the armamentarium against this lethal disease.
